utterances.text: Correct. And I have already explained the manner in which I reached that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly, that conclusion was also drawn from decisions on salaries that you saw. Is that where you drew that conclusion from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In the list of additional sources you provided to us, you didn't list decisions on salaries. Of course, I don't have an English translation, so I'm doing my best with the B/C/S. But you listed the four documents we've been discussing, three collections of per diems -- no, four collections of per diems. That's all you listed. So can you clarify for us which documents you relied upon to cite the rules on the salaries of workers of the JATD?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. Well, for example, the decision in which Milan Radonjic was given a salary coefficient, which was 4.43. According to this decision, the salary was paid from the 1st of December, 1993. In the statement of reasons provided in this decision, it says the level of the coefficient, 4.43, was established on the basis of the decision on appointments and on the basis of Articles 4, 5, and 6 on the salaries of staff members of the unit, and so on and so forth. So one can't doubt the existence of those rules. Otherwise, how would it have been possible for there to be a reference in the decision to something that didn't exist? And we have the same case that concerns Milenko Milovanovic. This is the second document. His coefficient was somewhat lower. It was 3.77.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt you. We have those documents. You've provided the answer. You got it from P2724; that is the decision your reading from for Milan Radonjic. And P481; that's the document relating to Milenko Milovanovic. So I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we have those materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, could I go back for a second because you are putting a lot of questions to the witness and sometimes he doesn't know how to answer which. You said: In this document, where's the basis for 27 posts? That was one of your questions. Well, if you look at the document, you find it easily, isn't it? If you look at the column "rules," you see that it always starts with Article 37, and that then slowly the number, which is the sub-column of the rules column, that apparently describes the item. Now if you follow that page by page, you'll see that at number -- at page 16 out of 17, you've reached number 27. So I'm both surprised by the question, because apparently what is described here is the posts as to be found in Article 37. Article 37, I'm not aware of. But that apparently 37 - and that also is a bit surprising on your question about 37 - throughout this document, Article 37 of whatever is used as the basis for his description of jobs. Whereas, under Article 7 [sic], slowly moving this document, we find 27 categories. So I both have problems with the question but also with the witness not being able to answer that, where it looks pretty obvious to me that if what we find in the report is taken from this document, then I have no great difficulties in finding it in the document. Unless my analysis is -- is made in error.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand your point. I take your point. One of the points I'm trying to make is that, of course, the witness doesn't cite to where he gets the information. You're absolutely correct, Your Honour, that there are 27 sub-numbers under Article 37, according to this document -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And always every new number gives another description.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then apparently there are several of such posts. Or at least that that description is valid up till the next item, which then gives a new description.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's how I understand this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's how I understand it too, and this is the only source we have for this. So ... But when you count up the individual entries, including all the numbers underneath, you get to -- what I got to was approximately 207. So the number 438 workers filled or not filled [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll have to -- I'll have to further analyse --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- is the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have to further analyse that, whether there's a logical explanation for that as there was for Article 37 and for the 27 posts. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all I would add to your analysis is something about the column, where the number of perpetrators, or, rather, the number of individuals is referred to, and this then clarifies everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, I would need a bit more time making additions. Whether we would come to that. So, therefore, the 438, the witness has not explained it, but it may well be that the document itself can explain it. We'll have a further look at it. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if Mr. Petrovic has any evidence in support of that, we would certainly be interested in seeing the evidence that he's referring to with respect to the number of executors, as it says in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that he's saying that it's found in the document itself. That's the evidence. We'll have a look at it. And let's not spend further time on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I would have expected the witness to be able to -- to deal with the matter in a second and guide you to where you can find what he most likely, if taken from this document, has summarised accurately in the report. At least the 27 posts are clearly to be found in this document. Again, whether the one document is a sufficient source for drawing these kind of conclusions is a totally different matter, but if looking at this document, it seems to be clearly as far as Article 37 are concerned, then 27 posts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In paragraph 375 of your report, you state that: "The position of commander of the JATD was never filled during its existence. And from 1 December 1993, the unit was under the commander of Milan Radonjic who had been assigned to the work post of deputy commander of the JATD." You cite in footnote 362 a document which is admitted as P476 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P476 but not broadcast it to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As you will see when the document comes up - perhaps you remember it since you used it yourself - this is a document which contains another two documents from Milan Radonjic's personnel file, that is, in addition to the one that you've been discussing with us which was P2724. Now, unless I am mistaken, which is certainly possible, I don't think it says in P476 that Radonjic was assigned to the work post of the deputy commander of the JATD. Can you assist me in telling me where in this document you found that from? This is a document you cite to that assertion.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. I was a bit confused earlier on. I'm surprised by the way I'm being asked about this because it's there in writing. I'll answer your question. This document says that Radonjic, Milan was assigned to a post under item 5, number 2 of the decision. When you have a look at P974, which is a document we had a look at a minute ago and it's a document I now have, we can see that this concerns the post of deputy commander. I'll show it to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see the name: Radonjic, Milan. When you compare the two documents, that's the conclusion I reached. But under 1, there is nothing. So the post of commander wasn't filled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, there were two parts of this that confused me, and that's why I'm asking for your help in understanding it. First you say item 5 instead of saying item 37, and that goes back to our discussion earlier. Then you don't cite to P974. Of course we have P974 - we can see it there - but you are drawing conclusions and we didn't know exactly where -- we had to do our own investigation in order to figure out where you drew your conclusions from. Now, where did you get the information that the position of commander was never filled during the JATD's existence? Is that also from P974? because the line is empty.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What's the date of the document, P974; do you know? It's undated. It's not a trick question. There's no date on. So I'm wondering how, from this one document which we don't know what time-period it's from, how do you know that throughout the entire existence of the JATD the position of commander was never filled, based on one document such as this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document in which reference is made to all the changes made. It is filled in when a certain decision is taken, and then various names put down. But this can change. One position can be filled, another can become vacant, and so on and so forth. So this decision, in my opinion, should state that the position was filled at a certain point in time. And then if there was a vacancy, that would have been deleted. So there has to be a trace. This is what led me to that conclusion. That's the logic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So your conclusion, if I understand you correctly, is that this document is from a late enough date that it would have referred back to anyone who was ever holding that position? So if it's empty, that means, in your conclusion, it was never filled. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't a document that is only used on one occasion. It's a permanent document. If there are any changes, they are noted in the document. So this document is used on a permanent basis. If anyone was appointed that position at any point in time, a reference would have been made to the fact. You can see that under 3, where it says deputy commander of the unit, and certain other names were added there at a subsequent date. And then the dates are also put down, the dates that concern the period during which someone was in a certain position. So in my opinion this is absolutely relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I see. So you're familiar with this kind of a document - do I understand you correctly? - and based on your familiarity with this kind of a document, what we're telling us is that that's what would be here in this kind of a document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P2730 but not broadcast it to the public. 2730.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you will see before you in a moment is another document from Milan Radonjic's DB personnel file. This is his employee evaluation form. Now, you said you did not see, nor did you ask to see, any other documents in the DB files other than those that were provided to you. As you can see, Milan Radonjic is, as you say in paragraph 375, he is described here as deputy commander of the JATD. The Prosecution's position is that the person signing as Radonjic's supervisor is Franko Simatovic. If you had been provided with this document by the Simatovic Defence, just as you drew inferences about positions from other documentation, you could have drawn the inference that the commander of the JATD post did not have to be filled because, effectively, Franko Simatovic was functioning in that capacity, couldn't you have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, it doesn't say commander. It says the leader of the organisational unit. That's the first thing. And then secondly, on what basis is the Prosecution claiming that this is Simatovic's signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an appropriate comment. The first one is okay, that Ms. Marcus has not quoted the document properly. You should not introduce any other comments. You can revisit the matter in re-examination. Ms. Marcus, could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, I drew a leap from what you said earlier. You said an organisational unit and a special police unit is the same thing, and so from that I drew the head the organisational unit to be the head of the unit that we're talking about. If I'm incorrect, then please let me know. But my question was: If you had been provided with this document, you could have drawn an inference, along with the other inferences you drew from other documents, that the position of a commander of the unit did not have to be filled because, effectively, Mr. Simatovic was functioning in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that. That's not the conclusion that I would reach. For someone to be a commander, it's necessary for there to be a decision appointing him to that position in the service. How should I put this? No one can have an acting position. It is necessary to be appointed to that position. And also, I don't know whether this is his signature. As I have already said, I'm not an expert in that. And then when it says a leader of organisational unit, I don't know what that means. Perhaps that's a different administration. I don't want to speculate about the matter. But there was thing I'm certain about. My conclusion would have been the same or would be the same because in his personnel file there is no decision, and this post referred to in the job specifications wasn't filed. So it's not possible for me to speculate, since there is no legal basis for something of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Or no legal basis that you have seen in the documents you were provided; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the personnel file or in the documents now mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 375 of your report, you state: "The assistant commander was Dragoslav Krsmanovic. The JATD was in Lipovica near Belgrade." Now, before I ask you how you know, if I understand you correctly you know that Krsmanovic was the assistant commander of the JATD because he is listed on P974 at that post; is that correct. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in the document P974 it actually says that Zoran Rajic and Dragoslav Krsmanovic each held the position of assistant commander of the JATD albeit it at different times. Why did you only make mention of Krsmanovic as assistant commander in your report, and not Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. There certainly is no justification, but it would more precise to say that during a certain period of time one of them filled that post and during another period of time the other person filled that post. But then I would have to refer to the exact period, and I'm not sure about that. Dragoslav Krsmanovic, well, that was legible for me. And the other name wasn't. But there were no ill intentions behind that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You could also have gleaned it from P477, which was the decision on appointment of Zoran Rajic to Article 37, number 3, which was one of the four documents you gave us as the sources that you used; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, I haven't even understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was P477 in hard copy provided to the witness? That one that came afterwards. I think it was. I have another copy if it wasn't. I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's the fourth decision that we gave to you, dated 20th of May, 1994, in relation to Zoran Rajic. We discussed it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I should answer. What exactly should I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I think I can leave the point. I think it's fine. Now, in paragraph 376 of your report, you finally cite to P974. You state: "The JATD comprised the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth departments for anti-terrorist operations which were divided into sections. The other organisational units in the JATD were the squadron, the group for securing and maintaining the unit facility, the group for communications, the technical service, and the group for administrative and other affairs." Now, again perhaps I missed it and you can assist. Where in P974 does it describe the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth departments?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed not to hit the microphones with the papers. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, would you please avoid touching the microphone with your papers because that hurts in the ears of the interpreters. Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In paragraph 376 of your report, when you say squadron, you mean air force squadron; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that because it's stated here explicitly. A avion mechanic, a pilot, well, that means that that person worked in some kind of an aircraft, something that would fly. It can't be something that goes underground.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In paragraph 388 of your report - that's the very last paragraph - you state that: "During its existence, 1993 to 1996, the anti-terrorist operations unit had a variable number of members, both in terms of overall complement and with respect to the number of persons on temporary contracts (up to six months) and the manning of the reserve JATD force." How do you know all of that information?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have partially answered that question already, but I will repeat what I said. The composition was variable, and this can be seen in this document P974. You can see that it hadn't been completely brought up to strength because certain positions remained vacant. And you can see that its composition were variable because some names were crossed out. Modic, Rade, for example, under number 12, he had trained to be a avion mechanic in secondary school. So you can see on the basis of this document that the composition is variable. And then as far as the pay slips for per diems is concerned, you can also see that the number of those pay slips also varied. Sometimes increased, sometimes decreased. So the essence of your question is how do I know that they were taken on a for six months and how do you know that it was a reserve force, well, I know that because that was the only way in which one could join up. No one could be engaged for a certain period of time that lasted for five years. For five years. In fact, it could be up to six months, according to the rules. And, finally, the reserve forces for the JATD were partially brought up to strength, and I don't see why that should be in dispute. The number of all these members was variable. I said that in response to a question that you put to me. So this would vary. The numbers would vary from month to month.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you gleaned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting. On page 62, from line 4 through line 9, where the temporary work is explained for a period of up to six months, maybe it is my problem, but I do not understand the transcript. It's -- it may be just me, but I need -- I think that this needs clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there reason to believe that anything is transcribed which the witness did not say, because you then have an opportunity, make a marking on the transcript, and clarify the matter with the witness. Unless, Ms. Marcus, you have problems in understanding this evidence as well, where, of course, it would ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Simply, the witness was speaking too fast, and I believe that the gist of his answer was misrecorded because of the speed at which he provided his answer. I apologise to Mr. Milosevic for having said that, but that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter may be of assistance: It might be clearer to say that the witness stated that no one could be engaged for a five-year period. According to the rules, they could be engaged only for a six-month period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this sufficiently clarify the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, may I urge you again to speak more slowly, because a part of your evidence might be lost if ... but we were able to justify the matter to -- to rectify the matter. Ms. Marcus, I'm looking at the clock. Would it be a suitable moment to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was just going to suggest that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then apart from that, I looked a bit more at the 438. Apparently what is the basis for the 438, unless I'm mistaken, that is the column called the number of executors. Now that gives numbers. Apparently four-digit numbers, which are not numbers of staff, apparently, but lower numbers, up to 50 or 53 or 52, sometimes 1, sometimes 2, so it -- it looks as if that explains how many of these posts were created. Adding them up, but I did it very quickly, brought me to 436, so there must be perhaps a small mistake here or there. At the same time, it is not easy to understand it because sometimes where the number -- well, let's say, 3 is mentioned, where you would expect, then, at the maximum three names, sometimes you find more names. So this leaves a few questions open. But apparently that's where the 438 comes from. I would agree with you that it should have been more clear and the witness should have been able to explain that immediately because he drew these conclusions. At the same time, a careful analysis of this document, before raising matters as unexplained and difficult to understand, might have saved some time and would have allowed us to focus on what then really remains as not fully explained in this chart and in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness is in the building. Should we keep him here or should we excuse him and ask him to come back tomorrow on whenever you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think asking the question is almost answering it. Ms. Marcus, I take it that you'll need a significant number of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you finish today?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I think that might be a little bit difficult, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time -- I'll discuss it with my colleagues, but it's not -- I know that I took a bit of time here and there, but I would have preferred that I would not have needed to do that, and I'm not always convinced, but I'll consult with my colleagues, that it was not also due to your questions that I needed to intervene. We'll consider it. But I think, for the witness, he will not start today. Could you give us any indication, Mr. Petrovic, on how much time you would need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 45 minutes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, any indication already at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I inform Your Honours a bit later, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the witness doesn't have to stay, to remain stand by. We resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, the Chamber has considered your observations that it might be difficult for you to finish today; nevertheless, the Chamber invites you to try to do your utmost best. So this is not that we'll stop you and -- but, at the same time, having considered the way in which the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination developed, that you should really try to do your utmost best to finish during this session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In paragraph 381 of your report, you mention operative checks. You say in footnote 368 that: "Assignment to the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia, including the JATD, could be only conscripts who had not been convicted of any crimes." And you then specify which kinds of crimes would have precluded membership in the reserve force of the JATD. In your review of the documents, and, as you say, incomplete records, to which you refer, did you come across any biographies which describe a JATD member's prior criminal activities, whether active or reserve?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, under the Law on Interior of the Republic of Serbia, nobody could be hired if they had a previous criminal record, which means that they could not have -- I did not look specifically for ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm going to stop you there. Would you please listen careful to the question. In your review of the incomplete records to which you refer, did you come across any biographies which describe a JATD member's prior criminal activities. That's the question: Did you come across such information in those files?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only file that I looked as a complete set was Franko Simatovic's file, so the answer to your question is no, I can't -- the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've not seen anything. I did not look at anything. I didn't look for anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the simple answer to the question was: No, I did not come across such information. That speeds up the examination. If Ms. Marcus would like to know more, she'll ask you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 6489 but not broadcast it to the public. That's 65 ter 6489. And I'd like page 2, please, in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you will see before you in a moment is an excerpt of a DB personnel file for Miomir Popovic. This document from his file contains a cover letter and a background check for membership in the JATD. This is another document similar to the kind of documents from DB personnel files which were given to you by the Simatovic Defence. As you see on this page, to the right of the document, there are handwritten notes, which say: "Has criminal record." And then just below that, it says: "Active, no." The signature that appears there or the initials that appear just above that writing, our position is that that is the signature of Milan Radonjic. You are not familiar with Radonjic's signature, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I please have the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And then I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Previous page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This is the cover letter to that background check. And here you see, again, in handwriting, "KE," which I believe stands for criminal record, and below that "reserve." And again the signature which we say is that of Radonjic. Just below that it says that the criminal record is a traffic violation and then it says: "Yes." So it would appear from this that when it was believed that Miomir Popovic had a criminal reported, he could be admitted to the JATD but only to the reserve force. But when it was discovered that the criminal record was only a traffic violation, he was then authorised for admission into the active JATD force. Now, our position is that individuals with criminal background could, in fact, and were, in fact, admitted to the reserve force of the JATD. Now, your assertion that individuals with criminal backgrounds were precluded from admission is also not based on any particular JATD documentation, but you base that, rather, upon the general MUP rules in this respect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the general MUP rules. However, I will provide you with a very detailed explanation and interpretation, if necessary, because I'm very familiar with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If the Defence would like to ask you more detail about that, then that will be up to them. For my purposes I would like to move on to another document and ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court officer please call up 65 ter 6448. This also should not be broadcast to the public, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm -- it might be useful -- I don't know if the -- it's been left so vague, the witness's answer. It's not clear whether he wanted to answer the Prosecution's question or wanted to elaborate on something else, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the real thing is, but we could verify that ... The witness said that it was on the basis of the rules that he made this assertion. Now, if he wants to elaborate on what the rule's exactly, I think what Ms. Marcus is interested to know is whether the witness has any factual knowledge which would -- which would shed light on what happened in practice, rather than to hear about the details of the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My concern was that his explanation might relate precisely to the reserve force issue rather than just the MUP rules, and I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that is -- When you offered to give a detailed explanation, was it again about the rules, or was it about any -- and if it was about the rules, would it be about the distinction between regular members and reserve -- the reserve force? Could you tell us what you had -- without giving the whole of the explanation, what it was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to explain the abbreviation of "KE," criminal records. I wanted to tell you that this is not relevant. I wanted to tell you what criminal records contain and put everything in the context so as to help you understand what we're talking about. I believe that everybody would welcome more light shed on the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you specifically deal with the difference, as far as the criminal records are concerned, the difference between the reserve forces and those employed on a more permanent, regular basis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this applied to everything. The background checks and vetting applied to both reservists as well as active-service duty personnel. What I'm saying is that things are not what they seem and what they appear on the face of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have factual knowledge on how it was done; or would you explain it on the basis of the rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar with all this because this is an integral part of what I used to teach as a professor. I'm familiar with the matter. And the matter is really very simple. It would suffice me to say a couple of sentences in order to explain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... why not answer my question, Mr. Milosevic? I asked you whether you had factual information on how it was done, in this context, who did it, how it was done, whether the rules were always followed or not, whether there were any deviations from the rules. That's factual information. Is it that what you want to present to us, or would you explain how the system was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to explain what the system was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I leave it to Mr. Petrovic to deal with the matter in re-examination, if he considers this to be relevant. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you see in front of you now is a page from the DB personnel file of Budimir Zecevic. Have you seen this document in preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was among the documents that you gave me. But when I produced my expert report, or, rather, before I produced my expert report, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's correct. This is one of the documents which is listed on the chart containing documents signed or initialed by Mr. Simatovic. Now, there has been evidence from a high-level JATD official that it was the practice that Mr. Simatovic would initial documents relating to the unit after they were signed but prior to them being sent out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is the 20th of October, 2011, at page 16463.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As you can see, this document, which we say was initialed by Mr. Simatovic, states that he received a handgun which was used by Budimir Zecevic in the commission of the crime of murder. Now, if you look at the rest of Mr. Zecevic's personnel file, you will see that he has no contract of employment with the JATD of the DB. Our position is that he was a reservist and that a criminal background would not have and did not prevent the JATD from recruiting him, or others like him, into the reserve force of the JATD. Would you like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, in linguistic terms one aspect of this document shows that this was not a member of the JATD. He was a member of the special units of the police of the Republic of Serbia. But I don't know why this is relevant. Is this relevant because it was signed by the chief of administration? That was Vlastimir Djordjevic who was in charge of public security. I'm not sure what your question is actually about. What I see up there is -- does not look like an initial. This looks like a Roman numeral II, plus 2, plus Franko, which might mean that he was familiar with the matter but he referred it to a different administration. I really don't know what these scribblings mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question, and that -- I think that would have been clear to you, of Ms. Marcus was mainly about admission of reserve force members who had a criminal record, whether you would like to comment on that. And this document is shown as one element in what the Prosecution claims has happened in this respect. Could you please focus on that. But, Mr. Petrovic, you're ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have missed something, but can we see proof that this person was admitted after the event, that he was a member of something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Petrovic, you may challenge that. That's fine. But you cannot, at this moment, intervene in this way in the cross-examination by Ms. Marcus. That's also the reason why I said "the Prosecution claims." Nothing more; nothing less. Any -- but that was apparently clearly the focus of Ms. Marcus's question. Could you comment on that, please, rather than on other matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This shows that the person who was already a member of the special units, at least how I'm reading the document, the person who was already a member of the special units of the police of the MUP of Serbia in the meantime committed a crime, a crime of murder. In my opinion, this person did not first commit that crime of murder and then was admitted as a member of special units. At the moment when somebody is engaged, you don't know in advance what they might do in the future. I believe that things here are a bit upside down. We're talking at cross-purposes here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I believe that the English translation has been released - I apologise if it wasn't released before - so that the Chamber can also see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, did any of the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have it on our screens since the witness is apparently making his comments on the basis of the precise text of the document. Therefore, I'd like to see it. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour? Or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did any of the documents which you were provided with, which you deemed irrelevant in preparation of your report, did any of them indicate that persons of criminal backgrounds were, in fact, admitted to the unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember having seen any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with this document. What was the difference between the tasks carried out by the active and reserve forces of the JATD; if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no difference. The only difference was the grounds for engagement. I'm not familiar. I don't know if they were any different, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In paragraphs 384 and 385 you describe the legal grounds for the minister of the interior to call up persons from the MUP reserve force. Then in paragraph 386, you return to the subject of the JATD. Are you saying that the active and reserve force of the JATD was staffed by individuals who were previously part of the MUP reserve force and who were called up by the minister of the interior for JATD duty?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about legal grounds, as you stated it yourself. And I believe that that says everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So your evidence is, then, that the JATD active and reserve forces were comprised of individuals who were previously MUP reserve force members. In other words, this was some kind of formal call-up by the minister of the interior for the JATD. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that. How do you make such an inference? I only told you that the legal grounds for engagement was Article 237, paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Law on Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, dating back to 1991, which means that, as it says in footnote 386, that JATD was a part of the reserve forces of the Ministry of the Interior, and only people who -- without any previous criminal record could be admitted, not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has actually made a difference between a criminal record and a criminal report. Due to the speed of the witness's speech, this was not recorded, and I believe that this part of the witness's answer was important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please resume your answer, where you said: "And only people without a previous ..." And then further repeat your answer. And in a slow way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be precise, I'm going to quote. And I will read slowly for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please say where he is quoting from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us from what paragraph you are quoting? He's apparently quoting from his report, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 384, footnote 368. "This profession meant that that was Article 27 of the Law on Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, and that was the system that was applied to recruiting everybody into both the reserve forces, as well as active-duty forces --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can read that. So you refer as the main part of your answer to footnote 368. Would you like to add anything to this, or is this your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to underline that the question put to me by the Prosecution, I don't know what the context of that question is, but what is certain is that those people were those people who did not have a previous criminal convictions for the crimes that are mentioned here, because if they had been convicted, they would not have met the criteria for admission. People from reserve forces were not recruited into the JATD because they were not linked. The only thing that they had in common was the same legal grounds, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm actually not asking you about the criminal records issue now. I'm trying to understand, and I still, listening carefully, I still am not sure I understand what you're saying in these three paragraphs. Paragraph 384 and 383 describe the legal grounds for the minister of the interior to call up members of the MUP reserve force. You describe the legal grounds in 384 and 385. Then in 386, you go on and discuss the JATD. Maybe it's directly implied, and maybe this is clear, and it should have been clear to me, but I'd like to ask you anyway, to just confirm for me, that what you're saying is that the JATD active and reserve forces were comprised and staffed by people who were previously MUP reserve force members, who were called up by the minister of the interior for duty in the JATD. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that. I only said that they had the same legal grounds, that the legal grounds based on which they were called up was the same. I really don't know where you draw your inferences from. I have never stated that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Then paragraphs 384 and 385 which describe the call-up of persons from the reserve forces, that's actually irrelevant to the JATD discussion; is that right, then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, there is a link, because all members of the reserve forces, and that includes reserve forces in the JATD, were in fact MUP reserve forces. So they had certain rights and duties that had been referred to. In Article 386, Article 28, item 4, the Law on Internal Affairs. But people weren't transferred from one unit to another, and so on and so forth. There's no link in that sense, and that's not what it says here. If that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's more clear. Thank you. Now, in your report, you only discuss the active, short-term, and reserve members of the JATD. You do not mention in your report other service providers or individuals who carried out operational duties as part of the unit. What other categories of service providers, by law, would have existed, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of there being any other categories of service providers. Do you have associates in mind? If that's the case, as I have said, they weren't part of the formation, so I'm not quite sure what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm thinking, for example, of Arkan's Men.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, someone who isn't part of the unit can't be a member of the unit. That's just impossible. It is necessary to have one of the decisions that we had a look at. Apart from these individuals who had decisions and who were referred to in the job specifications, there were no JATD members. There was no one who performed duties of any kind within the JATD without such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So your last comment: "There was no one who performed duties of any kind within the JATD without such documents." I'm not asking you only about members; I'm asking you about individuals who were carrying out operational duties for the unit, who were paid for those tasks by the unit, and what rules those people would have fallen under.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer in a hypothetical way because I don't have any specific information about that. If the Chamber agrees, that is what I'll do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes. What would be the rules for persons who were carrying out operational duties for the unit and were paid for it but were not members? Were there any rules for that or -- it's, I would say, a rather theoretical question than a hypothetical. Unless those persons did not exist. But that's a factual matter. We are talking about, I take it Ms. Marcus is interested to know, under what rules they were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of the possibility of someone who isn't part of the service receiving a salary. There were external associates, and that is the case in all parts of the RSB [as interpreted]. That was also the case for the public security system. And occasionally they would be remunerated. I provided detailed explanations about that. This was done on the basis of the rules of work. But for someone to be in the unit without a decision to that effect, well, I quite simply don't see how that would be possible. It's theoretically impossible. I'm not familiar with any such cases. If we are dealing with a member of the unit, then the rules of work apply to him. If we have someone who is not a member of the unit in question, I don't see upon which basis that person could be paid a salary, since there would be no decision on such an individual's salary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before I ask you a follow-up question, perhaps I could engage the assistance of the interpreters. We've had this come up before where I used the word in English "payment" and I believe -- and that's a neutral word which doesn't imply what kind of -- it doesn't mean salary, it doesn't per diem. It's neutral. It could be all of those. It could be per diem. It could be salary. I think there are two different words in B/C/S, so that's the word that I was seeking to use. Not to mislead the witness into thinking I was asking about salary payments.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Salary in B/C/S would be "placa;" whereas remuneration, compensation could be "naknada" in B/C/S, or "reward."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you answered the question, you were using the word salary. Would your answer cover also other types of remuneration, compensation, whatever? It's about receiving money for what you do. That's what Ms. Marcus was asking about, irrespective of whether you were formerly employed by the service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a big difference between salaries and per diems, and that kind of remuneration on the one hand, and the -- and sort of rewards for associates, that's something else. Associates could sometimes be remunerated. They could be given certain funds that were deemed to be appropriate. But as for salaries and everything else, and these things are paid on a regular basis in accordance with the rules and certain contributions made from such salaries, taxes paid, and so on and so forth, taxes deducted from such salaries, so only a member of a unit could be paid such a salary if such a member had a decision pursuant to which he was made a member of the unit in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you reviewed payment lists, JATD payment lists, from 1993 to 1995. Did you notice that on many of those payment lists were lists of Arkan's SDG members receiving payments including on the lists which were signed by Mr. Simatovic for Milan Radonjic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who of those who were signatories were members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards. I have no information about that. But as for these lists for per diems, when you sign for these per diems, sometimes one person signs for several individuals. But even if that was done, I really don't know who was a member of that unit, and I can't testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Well, you know Milorad Ulemek. He's quite a publicly well-known figure; correct? And his name appears at the top of the list with the Tigers in each payment list. So if you had seen his name, you would have probably known; isn't that correct? Yes or no, please. I don't want to dwell on this. I'm going to move on. But I just want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, sorry, could I object to the question. There's -- if my learned friend is going to input a massive presumption into the question, i.e., that Ulemek was well-known and a public figure in 1994, then he ought to have a chance to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you familiar with the name of Milorad Ulemek, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you notice that his name appeared on payment lists that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall having seen his name. I wasn't really paying attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to have an SDG member at the same time being admitted in the JATD?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the answer to that question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about SDG members being admitted to the JATD, whether they should have or not, but are you aware of any such thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in part -- the way part 9 of your report reads, that's the JATD part, the reader would be led to believe that the JATD was an entirely new unit, newly formed, newly constituted, with no past operational history prior to its formation in August of 1993. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In the documentary evidence you reviewed in preparation for your report, did you see any documentation indicating prior operations carried out by individuals who were then formally reorganised of officially named the JATD? Individuals or groups.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that I have seen anything of that kind. I'm not aware of the fact or I have no information according to which there was a group of some kind that existed earlier. I really don't know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P2770 but not broadcast it to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you will see in a moment is another document from the DB personnel file of Milenko Milovanovic. One of the documents you say you based your conclusions on in the JATD section is a document from Milenko Milovanovic's personnel file. What I'm showing you now is another document from that same file. Now, you testified earlier, I believe, that you did not ask for nor were you provided with any other documents from Milenko Milovanovic's personnel file; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I never looked at such a document. And I have never seen this one before either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As you can see from this document, Milenko Milovanovic is requesting admission into the active service of the special-purpose unit, JPN, stating that since the 4th of October, 1991, he worked together with members of the JPN of the republican Ministry of the Interior of Serbia. For your information, Zoran Rajic's DB personnel file, from which you were given also one document which you used to draw inferences, also contains a document, stating that on the 1st of September, 1992, he joined the Republic of Serbia MUP special-purposes unit. This document was contained in the continuity of the unit chart which I gave to you with underlying documents under Zoran Rajic's documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's P2746.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You do not make mention in your report of the special-purpose unit of the MUP of Serbia prior to the formalisation of the JATD. How does this special-purpose unit fit into the MUP structures you describe in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, let me first respond to another part of your question. You have the right, I believe, to put leading questions to confuse me, to make me answer questions that I don't want to answer, and so on and so forth, but you can paraphrase things in a somewhat different manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have the supervision of the examination. There's no need to accuse Ms. Marcus of confusing persons. Would you please answer the question. And if there's anything that you'd like to observe but then different from what you just did, what you need to observe for us to understand your answer, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Well, as for the comment, I didn't say that I based my report on Milenko Milovanovic's personnel file. The personnel file includes numerous documents. I didn't have a look at that. His personal file is not something that I consulted because I didn't believe that that was necessary. I only saw the document that we have already discussed here, a document that we have already seen, and I spoke about that. So that was the first thing. If there was some misunderstanding, I do apologise to the Court and to the Prosecution. Perhaps the interpretation was wrong. As far as this unit we are discussing is concerned, as far as I know at the time there was only one unit within the Ministry of Internal Affairs. And later it was renamed the special anti-terrorist unit, SAJ. This unit was formed in the mid-1970s at an earlier date, it still functions, so perhaps that's what was in mind. But I haven't heard of a special-purpose unit of any kind that preceded in a certain sense the JATD. The JATD, in my opinion, was formed on the basis of the rules that I have already mentioned, but I know nothing about this request to join the active force that was submitted by Milenko Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get back to what really the question was. Special-purpose unit in existence before the JATD in August 1992 was established, as you said. Are you familiar with that, the special-purposes unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what sort of a unit that is. I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because earlier Ms. Marcus asked you, Do you know of any persons or groups of persons who do -- who would perform similar tasks as were performed by the JATD once it was established? And then you said to Ms. Marcus, I don't know what you mean. What do you have on your mind? Although the Chamber is usually more interested in what the witness has on his mind than what the examiner has on its mind. Then in the next question Ms. Marcus hinted at the possibility that the special-purpose unit might have been the predecessor of the JATD due to perhaps being composed of the same persons which later functioned in the JATD. Now, that's the context of the issue raised by Ms. Marcus. Could you tell us -- you have told us now that you are not familiar with the special-purposes unit, which also means, I take it, that you would not know persons serving in that unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, I think we have dealt with the matter. I apologise for now and then intervening, but we have to move on one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I appreciate your help, Your Honour. Thank you. Could the Court Officer please call up P2772 but also not broadcast it to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, this is another document which was contained in the chart which I provided to you containing documents with Mr. Simatovic's initials or signature on it. This document also comes from the personnel file of Milenko Milovanovic. And this document is signed at the end - if we go to the end of the document, please - by Dragoslav Krsmanovic, who you said in your report at paragraph 375 was the assistant commander of the JATD. Now, assuming that you are correct, that the JATD was officially formalised and established as per the 4th of August, 1993, this document, P2772, dated the 16th of August, 1993, post-dates the establishment of the JATD. Now, it is a request by Krsmanovic for a background check on 31 candidates for active and reserve duty in the JATD. This list of persons with background checks can be found in many of the DB personnel files for these individuals that you see listed here, but this one, as I said, comes from the personnel file for Milenko Milovanovic, whose name appears at number 14 on this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I request, please, that we return to the signature page. It's page 3 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As you see here on the last page the stamp, which appears on the signature of Dragoslav Krsmanovic, is the JPN stamp, the special-purpose unit stamp. Our position, as presented by His Honour Judge Orie, according to the evidence presented in this case is that the JATD was simply a reorganisation of a unit which, de facto, if not de jure, existed prior to the official formation of the JATD. One example of this continuity is the use of the JPN stamp on early JATD documents, such as this one. In preparation for your report, did you see other JATD documents with JPN stamps on them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If you had seen other JATD documents with the JPN stamp on them, would this have alerted you to the importance of discussing the JPN in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no. My answer is no. Because the unit was officially formed on that date, on the 4th of August, 1993, as it says here. So that is the period I took into consideration, the period that started as of that date. I don't see why I should have concerned myself with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, could I ask you the following. If you're reconstructing events, and if you are very focussing on the rules, wouldn't it be a rule that you used the stamp which relates to your own organisation and not just another stamp? Would that be a kind of a general rule to be applied? Don't use stamps of your neighbours but use your own stamps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't know how to explain this. I don't see how it is possible to use the stamp of some other body. That is against the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently here, if this is an authentic document, apparently people were acting against the rules.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if it is this kind of violation of the rules, that is, using stamps of other organisations, would not the first thing that comes to your mind is: Why would you be in possession of such a stamp; and what is the link between the organisation to which the stamp belongs and the organisation which apparently issues this letter or this document? Wouldn't that be the logical -- wouldn't that be the logical thoughts that would come up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it would be logical. But the first thing I would think about is the authenticity of the document that has been certified by an inappropriate stamp. But, in any event, I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's, of course, the question whether the glass is half full or half empty, is the document not authentic because there's the wrong stamp on it, or is there something else wrong with the document. Let's not discuss it. Ms. Marcus, I continued on what was a purely hypothetical question, "what would you do if." Usually it doesn't help that much, although sometimes perhaps a bit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will. Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 6485. This is one of the demonstrative exhibits that we provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you will see before you in a moment is one of the charts which we provided to you as an index to the underlying materials that we asked you to review last week. Now, to ensure that there's no confusion about what we say is represented in this chart: In the left column are the names of individuals whom we say were members of the special-purpose unit of the Serbian DB which we say was later renamed the JATD, and later yet, the JSO. The individuals on this particular list were killed while carrying out combat operations in Croatia or Bosnia as part of the DB special unit prior to the formalisation of the JATD. Now, the evidence in support of the fact of their deaths, the date and place of their deaths, the payments made to their families by the JATD later, and other related documents -- documentation, is cited in this chart, and the materials cited were among those you reviewed in a binder connected to this chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to leap up. I do have a submission about the approach by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first like to know what the question will be and then I give you ample opportunity before the witness answers the question. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to go to one of the examples directly with underlying documents. I was moving from the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what would you then like to ask to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I answer the question out of the hearing of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, before he answers the question, he would have to hear it anyhow. But the question -- if you think that it's -- it's really necessary, we'll invite the witness to leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, perhaps I could ask the question and the witness could be instructed to pause instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer the question which Ms. Marcus will put to you, first wait so that Mr. Jordash has had an opportunity to object to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, although I think my submission will have be to made in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, now from both sides. Yes. If you would remain stand by, the usher will accompany you for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I suggest that we first hear what Ms. Marcus intended to ask and that we'll then hear your comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to call up -- use one example of one of these killed members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Call up an underlying document from his personnel file and ask the witness -- well, I had one brief question about his -- his position that he was assigned. And then I was going to ask about the -- that the DB would only provide an award or a commendation to someone for combat -- for participation in combat operations in Croatia and Bosnia in 1992 if that person had been participating in combat operations on behalf of or for the DB. And a similar question about the payments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, so the first question would be: Do you have any knowledge about the award system in -- within the service? The second would be: Are you familiar with awards -- I mean, this is all in evidence, and I'm -- I have difficulties in understanding how the witness could add anything to this, and therefore I think that's the first thing that should be explored if you want to put this to the witness. I would not be surprised if the witness says, I've no knowledge about that, and then we'll just have this evidence and it -- it is not directly touched upon in the -- in the report, I think. Award systems?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the payments are. I think you're quite correct that the award itself is -- I don't think it is actually. The underlying premise of all of this is what the witness has excluded from his report, in our submission, glaring examples of a continuity of the unit from early on, and that's why we provided him with the materials, to give him an opportunity to say if he had these, he would have had to include something about the existence of the unit throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, it may be clear that the basis for the report is really very narrow. And whatever evidence we have about the continuity, the witness doesn't even know about the special-purposes unit to exist. So, therefore, it's clear that the witness cannot tell us anything about that, and that, of course, may limit or even strongly limit the probative value of his report. Apparently he was able to reproduce a lot of rules and legal texts, and it has become clear over the days that he has very limited knowledge on anything outside of that. Now we are exploring that if he would have known this, would you have -- it's -- it's -- it is a similar remark as I made earlier. Let me just confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers this exercise useless, not to assist the Chamber, unless in one or two questions you could establish that the witness has any specific knowledge about rules and awards and any specific knowledge on awards being given to members of the -- whatever unit for having served in Bosnia or Croatia. If you would establish that first and if the answer is in the affirmative, then we can consider whether or not to go this route, but we have too often gone in the same direction and to no avail. Mr. Jordash, I already said what -- without having heard what you wanted to submit. If there's anything in addition, because that -- we formed our opinion at this moment, we thought not detrimental to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. And it -- that was one aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I would add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's anything else you would like to add, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm duty-bound to put on the record the issue of notice. My learned friend just began her summary of the Prosecution position in relation to the members of the JATD, their operations, as indicated, according to the Prosecution view, by the footnoted material in the chart, and their receipt, accordingly, of benefits, as a result of being in that unit. That is information, we submit, should have been indicated in -- in the -- in the clearest of terms in the terms that the Prosecution have just indicated three years ago. One month before the end of the case, the Prosecution, for the first time, indicat the membership of this unit. And I -- I'd indicate that these -- this evidence footnoted in this chart is the evidence that they were engaged in operations. And I add to this submission my submissions that I made on the 29th of February, where the Prosecution indicated, again for the first time, that the payment lists were not a record of the JATD or not only a record of the membership of the JATD but were also something else, and a record of other people employed by the DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, admission of the chart is still to be discussed, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But it -- it's -- yes. And my submission is they relate to that but they also relate to what I must put on the record for the future, which is that in our submission the jurisprudence is clear that if the Prosecution are going to advance a case that there was a unit with a set number of people and that set number of people can be identified and those people went on and committed crimes, that's information we ought to have known at the beginning of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's on the record. Ms. Marcus, would you want to respond? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Briefly on that, Your Honour. As far as I recall from that conversation, what we decided was that Mr. Jordash would file a written submission on the issue of notice that we could respond to. If that's not the case, then we would file a written response on the issue of notice, as raised on the 29th of February and as raised today. And the only reason we haven't done so yet is because we were waiting for a written submission on that. So that's with respect to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the procedural aspect of a procedural issue. Then I don't think that at this moment you have put on the record what you would like to put on the record. Perhaps you further discuss with Ms. Marcus who is the next one to -- to move. And perhaps we could call the witness again to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, would -- sorry, Your Honour, would the -- my learned -- it's not my understanding we had a submission to make. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But please discuss this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with Ms. Marcus, and let's have the witness in again. May I make one general observation. If someone presents a report to say what is relevant for the report is mainly what is not in the report, then, of course, there's an unlimited area to discuss, unless there are good reasons to believe that it would have been appropriate to be there in the report, and that would be based on both what the report pretends to be and what is the factual circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Milosevic. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before I ask you further questions, could you tell us whether you are familiar with the rules and regulations governing the granting of awards? And I use that term most broadly. Awards, commendations, any kind of recognition to individuals. Are you familiar with the rules in the MUP generally governing the granting of awards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any specific set of rules or set of regulations that would govern that. But obviously there was grants for rewards or commendations or citations. However, I can't really give you any specific book of rules under any specific numbers that would apply to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Then let me ask you one question about remuneration and then I will move on. Pursuant to the rules, if someone was paid out of the RDB budget, they must necessarily have been carrying out tasks in connection with the RDB. It seems like an obvious question, but could you tell me if that's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say RDB budget? The RDB did not even have its own budget. It was the budget of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If someone was paid out of the budget of the Ministry of the Interior, they must necessarily have been carrying out tasks in connection with the Ministry of the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be logical, wouldn't it? But not necessarily. I don't know any details, so I really can't answer your question by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Last week His Honour Judge Orie asked you: "I'm interested in any knowledge you may have, and you may have had before you arrived in The Hague, about any personal dealing or any personal involvement of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic with the JATD. That's my question." And you answered: "They were certainly linked to that, but I don't know what facts we're talking about." What did you mean when you said "they were certainly linked to that"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by virtue of their position they must have been linked in some way. Somebody who is chief of department and someone who is a special advisor and prior to that a chief… or who occupies a certain position, let's put it that way as I can't reconstruct that now exactly off the top of my head… in any case, their position in the service was such that they were supposed to be familiar with all the elements, at least when it comes to Stanisic, he had to know all the elements of work of the Service. And I believe that Simatovic, as a special advisor, also had to be familiar with all the elements of the intelligence work, including these elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If I'm correct - and now I am asking you about your factual knowledge; your answer just now was an inference - you don't have any personal, direct, factual knowledge of the involvement of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic in the JATD. Did I understand your answer to the Chamber correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any personal knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Laugel to play a clip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that will have to be done tomorrow. Look at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just for your information, I have very few questions left. I would say less than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than ten minutes. So that is -- the Chamber appreciates your efforts to try to finish today. I would first like to instruct the witness not to speak or communicate in any other way with anyone about your testimony. We'd like to see you back tomorrow. As matters stand now, I take it that we'll -- we should easily conclude your testimony tomorrow. We'd like to see you back at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom. I would first want to invite the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom before we adjourn. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, because I would like to make one brief observation about the personnel file of Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Petrovic cried out for help and said, Where is the evidence that he was recruited? et cetera. The witness, in his answer, said, Well, the document doesn't seem to refer to any recruitment. It may be clear to you that the text of that document, if I hear what you said, is that -- it was the document about the -- about the -- the gun used in a crime. The -- you used it in a context of recruiting persons with a criminal background. I take it that you would at least be alerted by what the witness said, and by what Mr. Petrovic says, that the document, without any further information about a criminal background, seems to be even contrary to recruiting but would raise perhaps matters like: would you fire someone who has committed a murder when he is a member of the reserve forces of the unit? But it does not in any way refer to recruitment. And I take it that you're aware of that. So that the context which you describe in your questions is not one that fits well into the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honour, and I understand how the context might have affected that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that there's other evidence. I've got no idea. But at least this document doesn't provide any evidence of recruitment with a criminal record. We adjourn. And we'll resume tomorrow morning, the 10th of May, at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom, II.
